record.original_question: If n is a triangular number, is the smallest equilateral triangle that can contain n - 1 circles of radius 1 exactly the same size as the smallest equilateral triangle that can contain n such circles?

evidence.quote: Particular case of Problem 4. Let n be a triangular number. The smallest equilateral triangle needed to package n − 1 circles of radius 1 and to package n circles of radius 1 is the same.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A positive integer $n$ is called triangular if $n = k(k+1)/2$ for some positive integer $k$. For each integer $m \ge 1$, let $T(m)$ denote the side length of the smallest closed equilateral triangle that contains $m$ pairwise interior-disjoint closed disks of radius $1$.

Prove or disprove: for every triangular number $n \ge 2$,
$$T(n-1) = T(n).$$
Equivalently, when $n = k(k+1)/2$, is the smallest equilateral triangle that can contain $n-1$ unit circles the same size as the smallest equilateral triangle that can contain $n$ unit circles?
artifact.status_search_result: This is the Erdős–Oler conjecture. It is known to hold for all triangular numbers up to small values (verified for n ≤ 15, with optimal packings established for n < 13 and for triangular n), but the general statement remains open. (Some recent preprints claim a full proof, but these are not peer-reviewed and the conjecture is still generally regarded as open.)

status_evidence.title: Circle packing in an equilateral triangle - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: A conjecture of Paul Erdős and Norman Oler states that, if n is a triangular number, then the optimal packings of n − 1 and of n circles have the same side length.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is the Erdős–Oler conjecture; remains open in general, verified for small triangular n.
